newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian foreign minister hits media on race row.
newsitem.headline: Australian foreign minister hits media on race row.

text.p: Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer warned on Wednesday Australia's international standing could be damaged by continued publicity for a rebel politician who has sparked a bitter and divisive race debate.

Comments by independent politician Pauline Hanson, from socially and politically conservative Queensland state, have been widely reported in the region, and Asian newspapers have criticised Prime Minister John Howard for failing to take a tougher stand against her remarks.

"It is true that the amount of publicity that seems to be associated now with Ms Hanson, if it were to go on for a considerable period of time, would begin to tarnish Australia's image in the region," Downer said in a radio interview.
Other government officials, including trade minister and deputy prime minister Tim Fischer, have warned Hanson's comments could damage trade with Australia's booming Asian neighbours.

Hanson, dumped from Howard's Liberal Party this year for controversial comments about aborigines, complained in her maiden parliamentary speech last month that Australia was being swamped by Asians and called for a halt to immigration.
Downer, emphasising the conservative Liberal-National government's condemnation of racism, said Hanson was receiving too much publicity.
"We will continue to make it perfectly clear that we are a government which abhors racism, absolutely abhors racism, that regards racism as downright immoral and offensive," he said.
"There is a clear recognition in the region that these are the views of an independent member of parliament, one independent member of parliament, which are getting unbelievable publicity," he said.
"At the end of the day, I think what surprises people in the region is the enormous amount of publicity within Australia that Ms Hanson is generating," he said on Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
Downer has written to the Bangkok-based The Nation newspaper rejecting as "inaccurate and offensive" an editorial headlined "Howard's silence endorses Australia's racist fringe".
"And if we are subject as a country to gratuitous and offensive editorials from anywhere, be it in Australia or be it overseas, then we will respond to that," he said.
